entries.clue: Maria or Dud left describing heraldry (8)

indicatorNotes.Dud: A dud is a thing that does not work as it should, so the letters beside it will not work in the order given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
l = left, the eighth letter joining the fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Maria and Dud walking out of the room, still talking about coats of arms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dud' sits beside Maria like a second nickname and is the instruction instead. Armorial bearings are the formal name for a coat of arms, so the definition is an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Armorial is the adjective for anything to do with coats of arms - armorial bearings, an armorial shield - which is the business of heraldry.

entries.clue: Alan's smashed up about the nose (5)

indicatorNotes.smashed up: Smashing something up breaks it into pieces, and pieces can be put back in any order at all.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters with the apostrophe counting for nothing
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Alan has come off worse in a brawl and taken most of the damage around his face.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition wants a describing word, not a part of the body: a nasal spray, a nasal voice. A possessive is a gift to a setter, since 's adds a letter and hides the join.
annotation.definitionFit: Nasal means of or near the nose - nasal passages, a nasal twang - so anything about the nose is nasal.

entries.clue: Test purity of tea? Almost unknown (5)

indicatorNotes.Almost: 'Almost' stops just short of the whole, so the word it governs turns up one letter shy of its end.

blocks.note: Assam is an Indian tea, and it arrives here without its last letter
y is the algebraist's unknown quantity, alongside x

annotation.surface: A tasting panel checking a brew for purity without being able to name the blend.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'tea' as a for-instance, so a particular tea has to be found. An assay office is where silver and gold are tested before they are hallmarked.
annotation.definitionFit: To assay a sample is to test what it is made of and how much precious metal it holds.

entries.clue: Dishing out for a lively party (7)

indicatorNotes.out: Out here means out of order, an instruction that the letters beside it are not standing where they belong.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Food being served up in quantity at somebody's celebration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dishing out' reads as one phrase, which is the disguise: the verb is the fodder and its little particle is the instruction. A shindig is the sort of party where the furniture gets moved back.
annotation.definitionFit: A shindig is a noisy, cheerful party or dance, a word that carries the racket and the crowd along with it.

entries.clue: German man - he has luxury car (4)

blocks.note: the pronoun taken as it stands
RR is the badge of Rolls-Royce, the byword for a luxury car

annotation.surface: A gentleman in Germany who has a Rolls-Royce on the drive.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash does the work of a colon: the definition stops before it and the building starts after. Herr is the German equivalent of Mr, the title on the envelope.
annotation.definitionFit: German uses Herr where English uses Mr, the title that goes in front of a man's name in that country.

indicatorNotes.odds: Odds are the odd-numbered ones, so the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters are taken and the rest dropped.

blocks.note: the odd-numbered letters of SPYTRAINAT, read straight through the word breaks

annotation.surface: Agents being trained up somewhere rural, with the trainers in disagreement.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At odds' pulls hard as a single phrase and the setter has split it down the middle: 'at' is the last of the letters to be mined and only 'odds' is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Syria is a country on the eastern Mediterranean, its capital Damascus.

blocks.note: to saddle someone with a job is to burden them with it
the stern of a boat is its back end

annotation.surface: A stern-looking pig being loaded up with something heavy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stern' is the back of a boat here, not the grim adjective the surface offers. A Saddleback is a British breed of pig, and the definition is one bare word at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: The Saddleback is a British breed of pig, black with a white band over the shoulders like a saddle.

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' says the answer is inside the words that follow, sitting there letter by letter in order.

blocks.note: an unbroken run starting at the fourth letter of 'kitsch' and stopping three letters into 'leprechaun'

annotation.surface: A tacky leprechaun ornament being hauled in from somewhere.
annotation.walkthrough: Schlep is Yiddish and long since at home in English: to schlep something is to lug it further than you want to. The word break between the two long words covers the join.
annotation.definitionFit: To schlep something is to haul it awkwardly from one place to another, which is what drag means.

blocks.note: first definition: something that takes no effort at all
second definition: the Christmas story acted out at school, a play performed by children

annotation.surface: A school Christmas production described as no trouble whatever to put on.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition asks you to stop hearing the idiom and hear two words: a nativity really is a children's play. The apostrophe goes unmarked, which is why (6,4) looks like two plain words.
annotation.definitionFit: Child's play is anything done without effort, and a nativity is literally a play put on by children.

entries.clue: Ten in play, very small scene (7)

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts what stands before it inside what stands after it, planting one set of letters within the other.

blocks.note: a play staged in a theatre is a drama
ten in figures is 10, which on the page is a capital I beside an O

annotation.surface: Ten actors crowded into a play that has only a tiny stage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ten' hands over letters rather than a Roman numeral: the digits 1 and 0 are read as the letters they resemble. A diorama is the modelled scene in a museum case, with its painted backdrop and tiny figures.
annotation.definitionFit: A diorama is a miniature scene built in three dimensions, a landscape or a tableau shrunk into a box.

indicatorNotes.changed: Something changed is no longer as it was, so the letters come out in an arrangement other than the one given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A thorn on a branch that has grown round to point somewhere else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Changed direction' reads as one phrase and the last word is the definition standing alone. Short anagrams of ordinary nouns hide well, because the fodder reads as a thing rather than as raw letters.
annotation.definitionFit: North is one of the four points of the compass, so it is a direction.

indicatorNotes.upwards: Something written upwards runs against the usual direction, so the letters are read back to front.

blocks.note: the face of a clock or a watch is its dial

annotation.surface: A playing card dealt onto the table with its face showing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Face upwards' is one picture in the surface and two instructions underneath: a word for face, then that word turned round. Placed and the answer are both past tenses, which is how the definition is checked.
annotation.definitionFit: To lay something somewhere is to place it there, and laid is the past form that matches 'placed'.

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' points at letters already sitting inside the words that follow, unbroken and in order.

blocks.note: the run starts on the last letter of 'mum' and crosses the apostrophe: muM'S Grub
the setter's warning that the answer is a set of initials rather than a word

annotation.surface: Whatever it is your mother has been putting in her cooking.
annotation.walkthrough: MSG is monosodium glutamate, the savoury flavour enhancer listed on takeaway packaging. An apostrophe is invisible to a buried answer, and so is the space after it.
annotation.definitionFit: Monosodium glutamate is added to processed and restaurant food to deepen its savoury taste, and it is sold and labelled as MSG.

entries.clue: Type of train from Leeds I vandalised (6)

indicatorNotes.vandalised: Vandalising something leaves it wrecked and its parts strewn about, which is what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A service out of Leeds that vandals have got at.
annotation.walkthrough: Railway people call a locomotive a diesel, so a fuel answers 'type of train'. Leeds is a city in West Yorkshire with a busy mainline station, which lets the place name sit quietly in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A diesel is a locomotive driven by a diesel engine, the everyday word for a train that is not electric or steam.

indicatorNotes.Oddly: 'Oddly' asks for the odd-numbered letters only - the first, the third and the fifth.

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of DUNCAN
the setter's warning that the answer is a set of initials rather than a word

annotation.surface: The strange announcement that one particular man has genetic material inside him.
annotation.walkthrough: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid, which is what the bracketed note is flagging. Nobody is odd for containing it; the oddness is in which of Duncan's letters to keep.
annotation.definitionFit: DNA is the molecule carrying the genetic instructions of a living thing, so 'genetic code' names it directly.

entries.clue: Point to small exam as the most pleasant (8)

blocks.note: s = south, one of the points of the compass
wee is small, Scottish in origin and used across Britain
a test is an exam

annotation.surface: A teacher holding up a short exam as the nicest thing on the timetable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Point' opens the clue where a verb belongs and is a compass point, the commonest way a single letter is clued. Three separate pieces run together with only 'to' between them.
annotation.definitionFit: Sweet means pleasant or agreeable - a sweet nature, a sweet day - so the sweetest is the most pleasant.

indicatorNotes.Not half: Taken as an instruction rather than as speech, 'not half' throws half the letters away and keeps the rest.

blocks.note: REFOCUSING loses its first five letters, exactly half of its ten

annotation.surface: A manager asked whether the business is refocusing and agreeing emphatically.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British for 'absolutely, yes', which is what the surface is saying and the opposite of what the clue wants. Half the letters go, and it is the front half.
annotation.definitionFit: Using something is employing it, putting it to work, and the two words swap over without changing the sentence.

indicatorNotes.rum: Rum is British for odd or peculiar, and letters called odd are not standing in their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: An order at the bar: beer for nothing, and spirits for nobody.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word is a drink or an order about drink, and the last is the one doing crossword work: a rum do is a strange business. To unleash a dog is to let it off the lead.
annotation.definitionFit: To unleash something is to set it free - a dog, a storm, a torrent of abuse - and let it go where it will.

entries.clue: Be at great length to have rightful place (6)

blocks.note: the verb taken as it stands
anything that goes on at great length is long

annotation.surface: Someone talking for hours in the hope of earning their place.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Be at great length' reads as one instruction to a bore and splits after its first word. The definition is a phrase because the answer has no one-word synonym worth the name.
annotation.definitionFit: To belong somewhere is to have a rightful place there - the chair belongs in the kitchen, and so do you.

blocks.note: first definition: fenced spaces for keeping animals in
second definition: a pen is a female swan

annotation.surface: Wire runs and cages put up to keep poultry in.
annotation.walkthrough: The four words read as one straight description, and the question mark is the only warning that the last of them is a second definition. A male swan is a cob and the female a pen.
annotation.definitionFit: A pen is a fenced enclosure for animals; a pen is also a female swan, so 'birds' names the creatures rather than their housing.

blocks.note: first definition: a small silvery food fish of the salmon family
second definition: the past tense of smell

annotation.surface: A fish that has been out of the water rather too long.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, with nothing joining them but the temptation to read them as one complaint. British English keeps 'smelt' alongside 'smelled' as the past of smell.
annotation.definitionFit: A smelt is a small silvery fish sold for the table; and smelt is the past tense of smell, so whatever stank smelt.

blocks.note: c = cold, the letter on a British tap
a rash is an outbreak on the skin

annotation.surface: An outbreak of colds that somebody set off without meaning to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cold outbreak' reads as one piece of health news and is two pieces of wordplay: the letter from the tap, then the thing on the skin. A crash is an accident of cars or planes rather than any mishap.
annotation.definitionFit: A crash is a violent collision - two cars, a plane coming down - which is the kind of accident the word names.

entries.clue: Chaotic ops eventually hold group of trees (5)

indicatorNotes.hold: To hold something is to keep it within you, so these words have the answer sitting whole inside them.

blocks.note: an unbroken run from the last letter of 'Chaotic', through 'ops', to the first letter of 'eventually'

annotation.surface: Disorderly troops who finally take a stand of trees and keep it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chaotic' looks exactly like an anagram instruction standing in front of three loose letters, and it is part of the hiding place instead. Nothing here needs rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: A copse is a small group of trees, a thicket smaller than a wood.

annotation.definitionNote: Swimming baths is the British name for a public swimming pool and keeps a plural form for a single building, so it answers a singular word.

blocks.note: first definition: the common fund everyone pays into
second definition: the water at a municipal swimming place

annotation.surface: A cat picking its way around the local swimming baths.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' is a cat in the surface and money in the clue: the pot chipped into for a bet or an office round. Swimming baths is what a British town calls its public pool, sign and all.
annotation.definitionFit: A pool is money put into a common fund, which is what a kitty is; and the pool is the water you swim in at the baths.

entries.clue: Ruin it all, not quite a sort of bliss? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase; the question mark licenses it, because the answer names which sort of bliss is meant in the stock phrase.

indicatorNotes.not quite: 'Not quite' falls short of the whole, so the word beside it turns up without its final letter.

blocks.note: to mar something is to ruin it
the word taken as it stands
ALL docked of its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone warned that they are about to wreck the lot, and that this is hardly happiness.
annotation.walkthrough: Marital bliss is the stock phrase being pointed at, which is why the definition names a kind of bliss instead of offering a synonym. 'Not quite' works on the word in front of it, so 'all' loses its tail and 'it' survives whole.
annotation.definitionFit: Marital means of marriage, and marital bliss is the set phrase for the contentment of a married couple.

blocks.note: Morse is the code of dots and dashes
l = left

annotation.surface: The last piece of a coded message still lying about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scrap of code' invites you to take three words as one phrase; only the first is the definition and 'of' is there to join it on. A morsel is a small piece, most often of food.
annotation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece broken off - a morsel of bread, a morsel of gossip - which is what a scrap is.

entries.clue: Impudent troops on outskirts of Salisbury (5)

indicatorNotes.outskirts of: The outskirts of a place are its outer edges, so only the outside letters of the word are wanted.

blocks.note: the SAS is the Special Air Service, the British Army's special forces regiment
the first and last letters of SALISBURY

annotation.surface: Soldiers camped on the edge of a quiet cathedral city.
annotation.walkthrough: Salisbury Plain, the open country beside that Wiltshire city, is where the British Army trains, so the soldiers and the place name sit together without a murmur. Sassy is cheek with some style to it.
annotation.definitionFit: Sassy means cheeky and bold in a lively way, the American cousin of 'saucy' and a fair match for impudent.
